oneliner.t: Austin-area Democratic state representative since 2019 and former middle school teacher who won the March 3, 2026 Democratic primary over U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett (52.4% to 46.2%) and faces Republican Ken Paxton for the U.S. Senate.

born.t: May 17, 1989, Round Rock, Texas (born James Dell Collins)

upbringing.t: His mother, Tamara, left his biological father when James was seven weeks old. Wikipedia describes the father as an abusive alcoholic. A few months later she married Mark Talarico, who adopted James and gave him his surname. He went to Round Rock ISD schools and graduated from McNeil High School. His maternal grandfather, Jimmy Causey, was a Baptist preacher in South Texas. He was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes in 2018, the year he was first elected. (These details come from one secondary source only.)

education.deg: M.A. Theological Studies (Master of Divinity begun, not completed)

career.role: Sixth-grade English language arts teacher (Teach For America)

platform.t: His August 2026 'New American Dream' plan would repeal tax cuts for the top 1%, create universal childcare and paid family leave, help first-time homebuyers with down payments, and cap credit-card interest rates. He calls trickle-down economics a 'false gospel.'
Universal coverage through a Medicare buy-in ('Medicare for Y'all') open to every age, and breaking up vertically integrated health-care companies.
An 'all-of-the-above' energy plan (oil, gas, nuclear, wind, solar, geothermal); suspend federal gas and diesel taxes; end tax incentives for data centers and make them pay for infrastructure.

Calls himself a 'border security Democrat.' Backs the bipartisan Dignity Act and pathways for some undocumented immigrants, and would redirect ICE funding. In January 2026 he called for prosecuting ICE agents who abused their power.
Supports a two-state solution and banning offensive weapons sales to Israel. Has accused Israel of war crimes. Refuses support from AIPAC and J Street.
Refuses corporate PAC money and says he returns checks from companies such as Walmart and Chevron. Frames the race as 'top vs bottom,' not left vs right.
Protect the Second Amendment and establish universal background checks.
Opposes private-school vouchers and education savings accounts.
Remove the Trump administration's tariffs on farm inputs.

promises.t: Repeal tax cuts for the top 1% and fund universal childcare and paid family leave.
Create a Medicare buy-in open to all ages.
Suspend federal gas and diesel taxes.
Refuse corporate PAC money and AIPAC/J Street support.

said.where: campaign launch, Round Rock (as reported by KXAN)

record.t: First elected in 2018 (House District 52) and serving in District 50 since 2023. That is four terms (2019–2027).

Donor-committee filings for his Senate committee in 2025–26 show no corporate or trade-association PAC contributions. The PAC money came from labor unions ($113,750), leadership PACs ($159,000), and membership, ideological and other committees. His earlier state House campaigns took money from Texas Sands PAC, a pro-gambling PAC funded by Miriam Adelson.

claims.claim: Said he was never treated at the Ohio mental-health facility named in online posts, and that he had the flu.
claims.short: Not in Ohio facility; had flu

record.t: The Lindner Center at first said he 'has never received treatment' there, and later cited patient privacy. He appeared publicly in Texas on Oct. 9 and 10. PolitiFact rated the claim that he was discharged from the center Pants on Fire. The flu itself is documented only by his campaign.

said.t: Pledged to refuse corporate PAC money.

did.t: FEC donor-committee data for his Senate committee shows no corporate or trade PAC contributions.

said.t: Disavows AIPAC and has pledged not to accept support from AIPAC or J Street.

did.t: Attended an AIPAC event in late 2019 with a supporter who became a major donor to his 2020 state House campaign. No AIPAC money to his Senate committee appears in FEC donor-committee data.

entries.t: Voted against a Texas ban on transgender athletes in girls' sports, citing the bill's scope.
Told Fox News he opposes transgender athletes in girls' sports 'if it endangers safety or fairness.'
On Fox News in September 2026 he said he had 'missed the mark' when he earlier said there are six sexes, and stated 'There are two.'
Pledged to refuse AIPAC and J Street support and to back bans on some weapons sales to Israel.
His website touted fighting 'Republican extremism' and efforts to 'bully trans kids,' and 'bold, progressive' legislation.
The redesigned site dropped the word 'progressive' and focuses on 'billionaire mega-donors' and 'top vs. bottom.'

effectiveness.sponsored_note: Lead author of nearly 200 bills, 16 of which became law (Texas Tribune count, via Wikipedia). Passed bills include HB 3012 (coursework for suspended students) and HB 54 ('Javier Ambler's Law'). His recess bill, HB 455, was vetoed by Gov. Abbott.

democracy.t: Helped organize the 2021 Texas House Democratic quorum break against the Election Integrity Protection Act (a state election bill). He returned to Texas early, arguing the walkout should end. He also joined the 2025 quorum break.

debates.note: Debated Jasmine Crockett on Jan. 24, 2026 (AFL-CIO, Georgetown). In the general election he challenged Paxton to three televised debates in July and to a Fox News debate in September, and on Oct. 8 he accepted Trump's call for a debate. None was scheduled as of Oct. 9.

note.t: Born in Round Rock in 1989 and educated in Texas public schools and at UT Austin. He was away for graduate study at Harvard (M.Ed. 2016). He lives in the Austin area.

checks.legal: CourtListener and Justia searches couldn't be run: this tool can only open URLs that appear in search results, so the 'courts' item is 'news'. News and Wikipedia showed no criminal charges, civil judgments or ethics findings against him. One related matter is not listed as a legal item against him: Attorney General Paxton, now his opponent, sued to remove Talarico and 12 other Democrats from office over the 2025 quorum break, and the Texas Supreme Court dismissed the case for lack of jurisdiction in May 2026. The FCC equal-time inquiry over his appearance on The View concerned the broadcaster, not him. Texas Ethics Commission records were not searched.
checks.foreign: FARA: exact-name check of the DOJ FARA bulk files (registrants, short forms, foreign principals) run 2026-10-13 found no row naming him. Financial disclosures (Senate eFD, Texas Ethics Commission) were not reachable, so foreign assets and income were not checked. News reviewed showed no foreign-government or foreign-business ties.

research_notes: MONEY: FEC totals (S6TX00479) run through 2026-06-30. The Q3 report (due Oct. 15) was not yet in the on-disk data. Committee-contribution and independent-expenditure data come from the FEC files on disk. fec.gov pages, the FEC API, Track AIPAC and OpenSecrets could not be opened, so super PAC funders, the small- vs. large-donor split, industries and in-state share are missing. money_history is marked 'done' on the strength of direct FEC data only. Track AIPAC and super PAC donor checks still need a human. This was his first federal race, so 2026 is the only FEC cycle. The Q1-26 figure of $27M is a lower bound ('over $27 million'). The Texas Sands PAC (state-level) amounts need a Texas Ethics Commission lookup. Outside spending: Texas PAC and No Going Back PAC report the same or near-same sums against Talarico and for Paxton, which is likely the same ads coded twice. Lower Costs Now both opposed Paxton ($5.17M) and supported Talarico ($3.55M). AdImpact puts total ad spending in the race above $247M. ISRAEL: AIPAC's endorsement page and Track AIPAC were not reachable. JACPAC lists him but no contribution amount was found. NOT FOUND: Reasoning Mind dates, M.A. year, campaign issues page, Senate eFD, Texas Ethics Commission filings, FEC RFAI status, photo. Also noted: the Free Beacon (2026-06-23) reported a buried campaign-site page with ad-messaging instructions for outside groups. That comes from a single partisan source and was not independently confirmed.
